notes:
1. Meaning of Corruption

Corruption means the misuse of:

  • Public office.
  • Authority.
  • Entrusted power

for:

  • Private gain.
  • Personal benefit.
  • Political advantage.
  • Financial benefit.
  • It is inconsistent with:
  • Integrity.
  • Accountability.
  • Equality.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Good Governance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Corruption → Misuse of Entrusted Power for Private Gain

2. Corruption in Public Life

Corruption in public life means:

Using public office or public authority for:

  • Personal gain.
  • Political gain.
  • Financial gain

instead of:

  • Public interest.
  • Lawful administration.

3. Meaning of Public Life

Public life includes activities of:

  • Public servants.
  • Ministers.
  • Legislators.
  • Constitutional authorities.
  • Government departments.
  • Public Sector Organisations.
  • Local Bodies.
  • Public institutions.

4. Expected Standards in Public Life

Persons holding public responsibility are expected to act with:

  • Honesty.
  • Integrity.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Impartiality.
  • Responsibility.
  • Commitment to public interest.

5. Corruption and Constitutional Democracy

Corruption weakens:

  • Democratic institutions.
  • Public confidence.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Economic development.
  • Social justice.
  • Rule of Law.

6. Abuse of Public Office

Abuse of official position occurs when a public servant uses authority for:

  • Personal benefit.
  • Family benefit.
  • Political advantage.
  • Illegal gain.

7. Bribery

Bribery means:

  • Giving.
  • Offering.
  • Receiving.
  • Demanding

an undue advantage in exchange for:

  • Official favour.
  • Official decision.
  • Improper performance of public duty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bribery → Undue Advantage for Official Favour

8. Nepotism

Nepotism means granting:

  • Employment.
  • Promotion.
  • Benefit.
  • Public opportunity

to:

  • Relatives.
  • Family members

instead of following:

  • Merit.
  • Fair procedure.

9. Favouritism

Favouritism means giving improper preference to:

  • Friends.
  • Associates.
  • Particular individuals.
  • Particular groups

without objective or fair procedure.

10. Cronyism

Cronyism involves giving unfair advantages to:

  • Close associates.
  • Political supporters.
  • Business associates

through misuse of public authority.

11. Embezzlement

Embezzlement means dishonest misappropriation of:

  • Public money.
  • Government property.
  • Public funds

that were entrusted to a person.

📌 Must-Memorise

Embezzlement → Misappropriation of Entrusted Public Property or Funds

12. Fraud

Fraud may involve:

  • False representation.
  • Forgery.
  • Deception.
  • Manipulation of records

to obtain:

  • Illegal financial benefit.
  • Personal benefit.

13. Extortion

Extortion means obtaining money or benefit through:

  • Threat.
  • Coercion.
  • Intimidation.
  • Abuse of official power.

14. Bribery vs Extortion

Bribery:

  • Undue advantage is offered or accepted for official favour.
  • Usually involves participation of giver and receiver.

Extortion:

  • Benefit is obtained through threat or coercion.
  • Often involves compulsion or intimidation.

15. Misuse of Public Resources

Public resources may be corruptly diverted for:

  • Personal purposes.
  • Political purposes.
  • Private commercial interests

instead of:

  • Public welfare.

16. Political Corruption

Corruption in political life may involve:

  • Abuse of political office.
  • Improper patronage.
  • Favouritism.
  • Defection motivated by personal gain.
  • Misuse of public resources.
  • Undue influence on administration.

17. Administrative Corruption

Administrative corruption may involve:

  • Bribery.
  • Delay for illegal payment.
  • Abuse of discretion.
  • Manipulation of files or records.
  • Favouritism in public services.
  • Misuse of procurement or contracts.

18. Lack of Transparency

Secretive decision-making can:

  • Conceal irregularities.
  • Reduce public scrutiny.
  • Increase opportunities for misuse of power.

19. Weak Accountability

Corruption is encouraged when there is:

  • Poor supervision.
  • Weak monitoring.
  • Inadequate audit.
  • Lack of responsibility for decisions.
  • Delayed disciplinary action.

20. Administrative Delays

Complicated procedures and unnecessary delays may:

  • Increase citizen dependence on officials.
  • Create opportunities for bribery.
  • Encourage middlemen.
  • Reduce efficiency.

21. Excessive Discretion

Uncontrolled discretionary authority may lead to:

  • Arbitrary decisions.
  • Favouritism.
  • Abuse of power.
  • Corrupt bargaining.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Discretion without Accountability → Higher Corruption Risk

22. Political Influence

Improper political interference may affect:

  • Appointments.
  • Transfers.
  • Contracts.
  • Investigations.
  • Administrative decisions.
  • Enforcement action.

23. Weak Enforcement

Corruption may persist where:

  • Investigation is ineffective.
  • Trials are delayed.
  • Punishment is uncertain.
  • Institutional coordination is weak.

24. Lack of Ethical Values

Weak commitment to:

  • Integrity.
  • Public service.
  • Honesty.
  • Impartiality

may contribute to corrupt conduct.

25. Low Public Awareness

Citizens who are unaware of:

  • Legal rights.
  • Service standards.
  • Complaint mechanisms.
  • Transparency laws

may become more vulnerable to corruption.

26. Economic Factors

The attachment identifies factors such as:

  • Poverty.
  • Unemployment.
  • Financial pressure

as possible contributing circumstances in some cases.

However:

  • Economic difficulty does not justify corruption.

27. Effect on Democracy

Corruption reduces:

  • Public confidence.
  • Democratic accountability.
  • Institutional credibility.

28. Effect on Rule of Law

Corruption encourages:

  • Arbitrary decisions.
  • Unequal treatment.
  • Abuse of authority.
  • Selective enforcement.
  • Illegal exercise of power.

29. Economic Loss

Corruption may:

  • Waste public funds.
  • Discourage investment.
  • Slow economic growth.
  • Reduce development expenditure.
  • Increase project costs.

30. Social Inequality

Corruption benefits persons able to secure:

  • Influence.
  • Money.
  • Connections

while disadvantaging deserving citizens.

It may widen:

  • Social inequality.
  • Economic inequality.

31. Effect on Public Services

Corruption may weaken delivery of:

  • Education.
  • Healthcare.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Welfare schemes.
  • Public Distribution System.
  • Public utilities.

32. Administrative Inefficiency

Corruption reduces:

  • Productivity.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Institutional morale.
  • Public trust.

33. Impact on Human Rights

Corruption may indirectly reduce access to:

  • Healthcare.
  • Education.
  • Justice.
  • Welfare benefits.
  • Public services.

It can therefore weaken:

  • Human dignity.
  • Social justice.

34. Corruption and Public Resources

Public money and public property are held for:

  • Public purposes.

Their diversion for private benefit violates:

  • Public trust.
  • Financial accountability.
  • Constitutional governance.

35. Constitutional Position

The Constitution does not separately define:

  • Corruption.

However, its principles strongly oppose corruption through:

  • Rule of Law.
  • Equality.
  • Accountability.
  • Judicial Review.
  • Transparency.
  • Democratic Governance.
  • Constitutional morality.

36. Public Office as Public Trust

The attachment's constitutional approach treats public authority as a responsibility exercised:

  • For public interest.
  • According to law.
  • Subject to accountability.

Public office cannot legitimately be converted into:

  • Private opportunity for gain.

37. Ethical Governance

Ethical Governance means administration based upon:

  • Moral values.
  • Integrity.
  • Public service.
  • Honesty.
  • Responsibility.
  • Impartiality.

38. Corruption vs Ethical Governance

Corruption:

  • Abuse of office.
  • Personal gain.
  • Secrecy.
  • Misuse of authority.

Ethical Governance:

  • Honest public service.
  • Public interest.
  • Transparency.
  • Responsible authority.

39. Good Governance

Good Governance promotes:

  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Participation.
  • Responsiveness.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Efficiency.
  • Equity.

40. Corruption vs Good Governance

Corruption:

  • Weakens institutions.
  • Reduces accountability.
  • Encourages secrecy.
  • Violates Rule of Law.

Good Governance:

  • Strengthens institutions.
  • Promotes accountability.
  • Encourages transparency.
  • Upholds Rule of Law.

41. Public Accountability

Public officials are accountable to:

  • Constitution.
  • Law.
  • Legislature.
  • Judiciary.
  • Citizens.

42. Importance of Transparency

Transparency requires Government decisions to be:

  • Open.
  • Fair.
  • Reasoned.
  • Accessible to scrutiny.
  • Consistent with law.

43. Preventive Value of Transparency

Transparency makes it more difficult to conceal:

  • Improper decisions.
  • Favouritism.
  • Financial irregularities.
  • Diversion of funds.
  • Abuse of discretion.

44. Article 14

Article 14 guarantees:

  • Equality Before Law.
  • Equal Protection of Laws.

It opposes:

  • Arbitrary action.
  • Abuse of power.
  • Unreasonable discrimination.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 14 → Equality + Non-Arbitrariness

45. Article 16

Article 16 guarantees:

  • Equality of opportunity in public employment.

It promotes:

  • Fair recruitment.
  • Merit-based public service.
  • Equal treatment.

46. Article 16 and Corruption

Fair public employment reduces opportunities for:

  • Nepotism.
  • Favouritism.
  • Arbitrary appointments.
  • Patronage.

47. Article 19

Article 19 protects important freedoms including:

  • Freedom of speech and expression.

This enables:

  • Public criticism.
  • Investigative journalism.
  • Public discussion.
  • Exposure of corruption

subject to constitutional restrictions.

48. Article 21

Article 21 protects:

  • Life.
  • Personal Liberty.

Corruption can indirectly affect Article 21-related interests where it obstructs access to:

  • Healthcare.
  • Welfare.
  • Education.
  • Justice.

49. Article 32

Article 32 gives Supreme Court power to issue writs for:

  • Enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

It enables judicial protection against:

  • Unconstitutional abuse of public power.

50. Article 39A

Article 39A directs the State to provide:

  • Equal justice.
  • Free legal aid.

This promotes access to legal remedies regardless of economic status.

51. Article 50

Article 50 directs separation of:

  • Judiciary.
  • Executive.

An independent Judiciary strengthens:

  • Fair adjudication.
  • Accountability.
  • Rule of Law.

52. Article 51A

Article 51A contains:

  • Fundamental Duties.

The attachment links ethical citizenship with duties such as:

  • Upholding Constitution.
  • Safeguarding public property.
  • Promoting harmony.
  • Striving towards excellence.

53. Article 53

Article 53 provides:

  • Executive power of Union is vested in President.

Its exercise remains subject to:

  • Constitution.
  • Law.

54. Article 154

Article 154 provides:

  • Executive power of State is vested in Governor.

State executive authority must operate:

  • According to Constitution.
  • According to law.

55. Article 265

Article 265 provides:

  • No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 265 → No Tax Except by Authority of Law

56. Article 266

Article 266 deals with:

  • Consolidated Fund of India.
  • Consolidated Fund of each State.
  • Public Account.

57. Financial Accountability under Article 266

Public money may be withdrawn and spent only:

  • According to constitutional procedure.
  • According to legal authorisation.

58. Article 267

Article 267 provides for:

  • Contingency Fund of India.
  • Contingency Fund of States.

59. Article 280

Article 280 provides for:

  • Finance Commission.

It contributes to:

  • Constitutional fiscal governance.
  • Distribution of financial resources.

60. Article 300A

Article 300A provides:

  • No person shall be deprived of property except by authority of law.

61. Article 311

Article 311 provides procedural safeguards concerning:

  • Dismissal.
  • Removal.
  • Reduction in rank

of specified civil servants.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 311 → Civil-Service Procedural Safeguards

62. Article 311 and Accountability

Article 311 seeks to balance:

  • Fair treatment of public servants.
  • Administrative discipline.
  • Lawful disciplinary action.

63. Article 323A

Article 323A permits Parliament to establish:

  • Administrative Tribunals

for:

  • Service matters.

64. Article 323B

Article 323B permits establishment of tribunals for specified matters such as:

  • Taxation.
  • Labour.
  • Land reforms.
  • Elections.
  • Specified property-related matters.

66. Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment, 1976

The 42nd Amendment:

  • Added “Integrity” to Preamble.
  • Inserted Fundamental Duties.
  • Expanded Directive Principles.
  • Introduced provisions concerning Administrative Tribunals.
📌 Must-Memorise

42nd Amendment → Integrity + Fundamental Duties

67. Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment, 1978

The 44th Amendment:

  • Restored democratic safeguards.
  • Strengthened civil liberties.
  • Reinforced Rule of Law.
  • Made Right to Property a constitutional right under:
  • Article 300A.

68. Fifty-Second Constitutional Amendment, 1985

The 52nd Amendment:

  • Inserted Tenth Schedule.
  • Introduced Anti-Defection Law.
📌 Must-Memorise

52nd Amendment → Tenth Schedule → Anti-Defection

69. Anti-Defection and Public Ethics

The source links Anti-Defection Law with attempts to reduce:

  • Defections motivated by personal gain.
  • Political instability.
  • Unethical legislative conduct.

70. Sixty-First Constitutional Amendment, 1988

The 61st Amendment reduced voting age:

  • 21 → 18 years.

This expanded:

  • Democratic participation.
  • Electoral accountability.

71. Seventy-Third Constitutional Amendment, 1992

The 73rd Amendment strengthened:

  • Panchayati Raj.
  • Gram Sabha.
  • State Election Commission.
  • State Finance Commission.
  • Grassroots accountability.

72. Seventy-Fourth Constitutional Amendment, 1992

The 74th Amendment strengthened:

  • Municipalities.
  • Urban Local Self-Government.
  • Local participation.
  • Financial responsibility.
  • Urban accountability.

73. Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment, 2002

The 86th Amendment inserted:

  • Article 21A.

It strengthened:

  • Right to Education.
  • Civic awareness.
  • Constitutional literacy.

74. Ninety-First Constitutional Amendment, 2003

The 91st Amendment:

  • Strengthened Anti-Defection Law.
  • Limited size of Council of Ministers.
  • Imposed additional restrictions on defectors.
📌 Must-Memorise

91st Amendment → Stronger Anti-Defection + Ministry Size Limit

75. Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment, 2011

The source links the 97th Amendment with:

  • Cooperative societies.
  • Democratic management.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability

subject to later judicial interpretation.

76. One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment, 2016

The 101st Amendment introduced:

  • Goods and Services Tax.
  • GST Council.
  • Uniform indirect-tax framework.

77. GST and Transparency

The source associates GST with:

  • Digital tax administration.
  • Electronic compliance.
  • Better audit trail.
  • Increased transparency.
  • Reduction of tax-evasion opportunities.

78. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, 1975

The Supreme Court recognised the importance of:

  • Citizens' Right to Know about Government functioning

subject to:

  • Constitutional.
  • Legal limitations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raj Narain → 1975 → Right to Know

79. Importance of Raj Narain

The judgment contributed to development of principles relating to:

  • Government transparency.
  • Public accountability.
  • Right to Information.

80. K. Veeraswami v. Union of India, 1991

The case concerned:

  • Corruption allegations involving Judges of higher Judiciary.

81. Principle in K. Veeraswami

The source states that investigation against a sitting higher-court Judge requires prior permission of:

  • Chief Justice of India

according to safeguards laid down by Supreme Court.

📌 Must-Memorise

K. Veeraswami → 1991 → Higher Judiciary + Corruption Investigation Safeguard

82. Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997

The case concerned:

  • Political interference in corruption investigations involving high public officials.

83. Vineet Narain Principles

The Supreme Court issued directions intended to strengthen:

  • Independence of corruption investigations.
  • CBI functioning.
  • CVC supervision.
  • Institutional accountability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vineet Narain → 1997 → Independent Corruption Investigation

84. PUCL v. Union of India, 2003

The attachment associates the case with disclosure by electoral candidates of:

  • Criminal cases.
  • Assets.
  • Liabilities.
  • Educational qualifications.

85. Importance of Candidate Disclosure

Candidate disclosure strengthens:

  • Electoral transparency.
  • Informed voting.
  • Political accountability.

86. 2G Spectrum Case, 2012

Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India concerned:

  • Allocation of 2G Spectrum licences.

87. 2G Judgment

The source states that Supreme Court:

  • Cancelled 122 telecom licences.
  • Found allocation process arbitrary and unconstitutional.
  • Emphasised:
  • Fairness.
  • Transparency.
  • Public interest.
📌 Must-Memorise

2G Spectrum Case → 2012 → 122 Licences Cancelled

88. Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2013

The Supreme Court held:

  • Registration of FIR is generally mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
  • Limited categories may permit preliminary inquiry.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lalita Kumari → 2013 → FIR for Cognizable Offence

89. Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI, 2014

The case challenged:

  • Section 6A of Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.

90. Section 6A Judgment

The Supreme Court declared Section 6A:

  • Unconstitutional.

The source links the decision to:

  • Article 14.
  • Equality before investigation.
  • Accountability of senior public officials.
📌 Must-Memorise

Subramanian Swamy → 2014 → Section 6A DSPE Act Unconstitutional

91. Coal Block Allocation Case, 2014

Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary concerned:

  • Allocation of Coal Blocks.

92. Coal Block Judgment

The Supreme Court held the allocation process:

  • Arbitrary.
  • Illegal.

The source states that numerous coal-block allocations were subsequently cancelled.

📌 Must-Memorise

Coal Block Case → 2014 → Arbitrary Allocation

93. Common Cause v. Union of India, 2017

The source emphasises that allocation of natural resources must be:

  • Fair.
  • Transparent.
  • Non-arbitrary.
  • Consistent with constitutional principles.

94. Natural Resources and Public Trust

The anti-corruption principle emerging from resource-allocation cases is:

  • Public resources cannot be distributed arbitrarily.
  • Allocation must serve:
  • Public interest.
  • Fairness.
  • Transparency.

95. Judicial Principles against Corruption

The attachment identifies the following principles:

  • Corruption undermines Rule of Law.
  • Public office is a public trust.
  • Equality Before Law applies to public officials.
  • Transparency is essential to democracy.
  • Public resources must be allocated fairly.
  • Independent investigation strengthens accountability.
  • Citizens have a Right to Know subject to law.

96. Prevention vs Punishment

A strong anti-corruption system requires both:

  • Prevention before wrongdoing occurs.
  • Investigation and punishment after corruption occurs.

97. Preventive Approach

Preventive approaches mentioned in the attachment include:

  • Transparency.
  • Ethical conduct.
  • E-Governance.
  • Simplification of procedures.
  • Audit.
  • Citizen participation.
  • Whistle-blower reporting.
  • Grievance redress.

98. Punitive Approach

Punitive responses may involve:

  • Departmental proceedings.
  • Investigation.
  • Prosecution.
  • Criminal punishment.
  • Recovery of loss

according to applicable law.

The attachment identifies mechanisms such as:

  • Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
  • Central Vigilance Commission.
  • Central Bureau of Investigation.
  • Vigilance Administration.
  • Whistle Blower Protection.
  • Transparency mechanisms.
  • E-Governance.
  • International cooperation.

Note

These mechanisms will be covered in detail in Chapter 23 — Anti-Corruption Measures to avoid duplication.

100. International Dimension of Corruption

Modern corruption may involve:

  • Foreign bank accounts.
  • Offshore entities.
  • Cross-border payments.
  • Money laundering.
  • Foreign bribery.
  • Concealment of assets abroad.

101. Need for International Cooperation

Cross-border corruption requires cooperation involving:

  • Investigation.
  • Extradition.
  • Asset recovery.
  • Mutual legal assistance.
  • Information exchange.

102. Important International Frameworks — Overview

The attachment identifies:

  • United Nations Convention against Corruption.
  • UNODC.
  • FATF.
  • INTERPOL.
  • G20 Anti-Corruption Working Group.
  • Mutual Legal Assistance.
  • Asset-recovery mechanisms.

Detailed institutional measures are reserved for the next chapter.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is corruption? → Misuse of public office, authority or entrusted power for private gain.

What is corruption in public life? → Use of public authority for personal, political or financial gain instead of public interest.

Who are included in public life? → Public servants, Ministers, legislators, constitutional authorities, Government departments, Public Sector Organisations, Local Bodies and public institutions.

What is bribery? → Giving, offering, receiving or demanding an undue advantage for an official favour or decision.

What is nepotism? → Giving jobs or benefits to relatives instead of following merit.

What is favouritism? → Giving unfair preference to friends, associates or particular persons.

What is cronyism? → Giving unfair advantages to close political, business or personal associates.

What is embezzlement? → Dishonest misappropriation of public money or property entrusted to a person.

What is fraud? → Deception, forgery or manipulation used to obtain unlawful benefit.

What is extortion? → Obtaining benefit through threat, coercion or abuse of authority.

What is the basic difference between bribery and extortion? → Bribery generally involves an undue exchange; extortion involves coercion or threat.

What are major causes of corruption? → Lack of transparency, weak accountability, administrative delay, excessive discretion, political influence, weak enforcement and weak ethical values.

How do administrative delays promote corruption? → They create opportunities for bribery and middlemen.

Why is excessive discretion dangerous? → It can lead to arbitrary decisions, favouritism and abuse of power.

How does corruption weaken democracy? → By reducing public confidence, accountability and institutional credibility.

How does corruption violate Rule of Law? → By encouraging arbitrary decisions, unequal treatment and abuse of authority.

What are the economic effects of corruption? → Waste of public funds, reduced investment, slower growth and weaker development.

How does corruption affect social justice? → It advantages the influential and disadvantages deserving citizens.

Which public services may be affected? → Education, healthcare, infrastructure, welfare schemes and Public Distribution.

Does Constitution separately define corruption? → No.

Which constitutional values oppose corruption? → Equality, Rule of Law, accountability, transparency, Judicial Review, public interest and constitutional morality.

What is Ethical Governance? → Administration based on integrity, honesty, responsibility and public service.

What is Good Governance? → Transparent, accountable, participatory, responsive, efficient and lawful administration.

To whom are public officials accountable? → Constitution, law, Legislature, Judiciary and citizens.

Which Article guarantees Equality Before Law? → Article 14.

How is Article 14 relevant to corruption? → It prohibits arbitrariness and unequal legal treatment.

Which Article guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment? → Article 16.

How does Article 16 help prevent corruption? → It promotes merit and reduces favouritism and nepotism in public appointments.

Which Fundamental Right supports public criticism and investigative journalism? → Article 19 freedom of speech and expression.

Which Article provides Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32.

Which Article deals with Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid? → Article 39A.

Which Article directs separation of Judiciary from Executive? → Article 50.

Which Article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A.

Which Article says no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law? → Article 265.

Which Article deals with Consolidated Funds? → Article 266.

Which Article deals with Contingency Funds? → Article 267.

Which Article provides Finance Commission? → Article 280.

Which Article protects property against deprivation except by authority of law? → Article 300A.

Which Article contains procedural safeguards for civil servants? → Article 311.

Which Article deals with Administrative Tribunals? → Article 323A.

Which Article deals with other specified tribunals? → Article 323B.

Which Amendment added “Integrity” to Preamble and Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.

Which Amendment strengthened post-Emergency constitutional safeguards? → 44th Amendment, 1978.

Which Amendment introduced Anti-Defection Law? → 52nd Amendment, 1985.

Which Schedule did it insert? → Tenth Schedule.

Which Amendment reduced voting age to 18? → 61st Amendment, 1988.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Panchayats? → 73rd Amendment.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Municipalities? → 74th Amendment.

Which Amendment introduced Article 21A? → 86th Amendment, 2002.

Which Amendment strengthened Anti-Defection Law and limited size of Ministries? → 91st Amendment, 2003.

Which Amendment introduced GST? → 101st Amendment, 2016.

Which case is associated with citizens' Right to Know about Government functioning? → State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, 1975.

Which case dealt with corruption allegations against higher Judiciary? → K. Veeraswami v. Union of India, 1991.

What protection was stated in K. Veeraswami? → Prior permission of Chief Justice of India for investigation against a sitting higher-court Judge according to safeguards laid down by Court.

Which is the most important institutional anti-corruption judgment in the attachment? → Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997.

What did Vineet Narain strengthen? → Independence of corruption investigations, CBI functioning and CVC supervision.

Which case strengthened candidate disclosure? → PUCL v. Union of India, 2003.

What information must candidates disclose according to the attachment? → Criminal cases, assets, liabilities and educational qualifications.

Which case concerned 2G Spectrum allocation? → Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, 2012.

How many telecom licences were cancelled according to the attachment? → 122.

Which case held FIR registration generally mandatory for cognizable offences? → Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2013.

Which 2014 case struck down Section 6A of the DSPE Act? → Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI.

Why was Section 6A struck down according to the source? → Differential protection from investigation based on official rank violated Article 14.

Which 2014 case dealt with Coal Block allocations? → Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary.

What did the Supreme Court hold? → Allocation process was arbitrary and illegal.

Which case emphasised fair and transparent allocation of natural resources? → Common Cause v. Union of India, 2017.

What is the most important constitutional principle in corruption cases? → Public authority must be exercised lawfully, transparently and in the public interest; public office cannot be used for private gain.
